name: Surjapuri
confidence_why: Only one source describes Surjapuri stress, Srivastava & Perumalsamy 2020, a short survey sketch from a single informant giving non-phonemic penultimate stress "in most of the cases"; nothing contradicts it for Surjapuri itself, although Toulmin 2006 reports initial stress in the sister Kamta-Rajbanshi lects Rangpur, Thakurgaon and Bhatibari and remarks that stress in this group has never been properly studied, and Wilde 2008 finds preliminary initial stress in Nepal Rajbanshi.
catalog_citation: Srivastava, S.P. & P. Perumalsamy. 2020. 'Surjapuri'. In Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India (ed.), Linguistic Survey of India - Bihar (foreword dated December 2020), chapter paginated 595-666 by running footer (604-675 in the volume's table of contents). New Delhi/Kolkata: ORGI. Open scan: archive.org item PARI.linguistic-survey-of-india-bihar (also censusindia.gov.).
catalog_locator: p. 608 by running footer ('608 | P a g e' of the archive.org scan; p. 617 in the TOC pagination scheme), section 2.1 Phonemic inventory, subsection 'Stress' immediately after 'Length' and before '2.2 DISTRIBUTION OF PHONEMES'
catalog_quote: Length Length in Surjapuri is not phonemic. Phonetically, however, it occurs and it is predictable and determined on the basis of canonical shape of the words. The vowels in monosyllabic words are uniformly long. Stress Like length, stress also is not phonemic. It is a co - occurring feature. In the words having more than one syllable, in most of the cases, the penultimate syllable bears the stress.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; in words of two or more syllables it falls, as a rule, on the penultimate syllable (hedged 'in most of the cases'; monosyllables carry uniformly long vowels per the preceding 'Length' paragraph).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'in most of the cases'; no exceptions listed and no examples marked for stress anywhere in the chapter.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated citation forms from one informant elicited in Kishanganj, Bihar, 2010). No phrase-level or intonation discussion. Confidence is medium because the chapter is a brief ORGI survey sketch with a single-informant base, gives no stressed examples, and its penultimate claim diverges from the initial stress reported for sister KRDS lects (Toulmin 2011 for Rangpuri/Kamta; Wilde 2008 for Nepal Rajbanshi), so it may reflect the default 'pan-Indian penultimate' template rather than measured data.
new_statements.identity_note: The LSI-Bihar chapter describes the Kishanganj (Purnea division, Bihar) Surjapuri of a single informant elicited in 2010, i.e. the core variety of surj1235 (Grierson's 'Siripuria/Kishanganjia'; Toulmin's KS lect). Ghosh 1974 calls the same regional speech 'Colloquial Bengali of Purnea' and treats it as a Bengali dialect; Glottolog files it under surj1235. The West Bengal (Uttar Dinajpur) and Nepal (Jhapa) Surjapuri populations are not covered by any opened source. Sister lects have conflicting reports: Nepal Rajbanshi rajb1243 (Wilde 2008) and Rangpuri/Kamta rang1265 (Toulmin 2011) are reported with initial stress.

readall_conflicts: No source opened contradicts the catalog for Surjapuri itself: Toulmin 2006 is silent on Kishanganj/Surjapuri stress. There is an area-level tension worth flagging: Toulmin (pp. 132-133) attributes initial stress to several sister KRNB lects (Rangpur, Thakurgaon, Bhatibari, variably Shalkumar), and Wilde 2008 (already held by the project under rang1265/related_rajb1243/) reports preliminary initial stress for Nepal Rajbanshi, while the only direct Surjapuri statement (LSI-Bihar 2020, p. 608, one informant, one short field trip) gives penultimate stress 'in most of the cases', non-phonemic. Toulmin's own remark (p. 140) that the synchronic conditioning of stress in KRNB lects has never been properly studied means the penultimate rule rests on a single thin source; it is not refuted, but it is unconfirmed by any second observer.

sources.note: p.608 (PDF page 625), sec. 2.1 'Stress': stress is not phonemic, a co-occurring feature; in polysyllabic words 'in most of the cases' the penultimate syllable bears the stress. Length likewise non-phonemic (monosyllables uniformly long). Data from one informant, one short field trip to Kishanganj, Bihar, in 2010 (footnote p.595). Syllable section pp.623-624 mentions 'stress patterns' only generically.

sources.citation: Toulmin, Matthew W. S. 2009. From linguistic to sociolinguistic reconstruction: the Kamta historical subgroup of Indo-Aryan. Pacific Linguistics 604. Canberra: ANU. (Kishanganj/Surjapuri = lect KS.)
sources.note: Comparative work; sec. 4.4.4 attributes 'initial stress' to some KRDS lects (RP, TH, BH) and its absence to BN, SH; the Kishanganj (Surjapuri) lect is not named in any stress remark; p.100-area notes that the conditioning of stress in KRDS lects has not been studied. Cites Ngwazah, Turner & Toulmin 2006 SIL sociolinguistic survey covering Surjapuri.

sources.citation: Wilde, Christopher P. 2008. A sketch of the phonology and grammar of Rajbanshi [Jhapa/Morang, Nepal = rajb1243]. PhD, University of Helsinki.
sources.note: Sister lect, not Surjapuri: p.32 'Vowel length and stress are not contrastive. Preliminary observations would suggest primary stress is placed on the first syllable.' Mentions Surjapuri only as a lect name. Noted because it conflicts with the LSI penultimate statement for Surjapuri.
